title: Origin of Nanoscale Degradation in Thermal Energy Storage Materials Using Environmental TEM
content: Thermal energy storage materials (TESMs) offer one approach to a long-duration energy storage solution that is required for a resilient electric grid [1]. Although large-scale demonstrations have shown the potential of TESMs to meet this requirement, various degradation phenomena currently hinder further development towards commercial adoption [2]. TESMs are broadly sub-divided into two classes, phase change materials (PCMs) and thermochemical materials (TCMs), both of which store and release thermal energy based on reversible endothermic/exothermic reactions [3, 4]. However, irreversible processes can build up from repeated thermal cycling leading to hysteretic behavior and reductions in system performance. Understanding the fundamental mechanisms driving degradation phenomena is a critical step towards developing effective strategies for engineering these materials for long-duration energy storage.
